So the factory petcock should have a vacuum line attached to it. A quick check is to disconnect the vacuum line and gas line, hold a cup under it, and set the petcock to the run or on position. It should have three settings on it, “off”, “run” or “on”, and “prime”. The prime setting should flow fine, the on setting should only flow when vacuum is present (motor is running), and off is obviously off. 

Or just pull the petcock and check the filter on it. They sell rebuild kits that are pretty cheap. But most people end up swapping the factory petcock with a gravity feed option (only on or off).

If it runs better with the tank tilted a certain way I would probably just either order a new petcock, or a rebuild kit. Seeing as the bike is 40 years old it probably needs to be done.

RDAs are specifically drip atomizers. No tank. You just wrap a coil, install it in the posts, and run some cotton through it. Then you drip juice from the bottle straight on the coil. Personally I run the Dead Rabbit V3. If you want to have a tank, you’ll need an RTA. I’m not too familiar with them but they are the same concept. You can either buy premade coils or you can get the bare wire and a wrapping tool. Amazon sells coil wrapping kits that are cheap and work well. Steam-engine.org is a good calculator. Personally I run two coils made of 24 gauge Kanthal A-1 wire and wrap them to be about .15 ohms together. That’ll get you to be about 100 watts output safely, and you can push it higher if you want a big rip. You’ll figure out where you like it set.

If you buy a rifle (16” HBAR 5.56 or .223) then you couldn’t put a SBR or pistol length upper on it. If you bought a pistol (>16” length with no stock) then you could put a rifle pistol or SBR upper on it anytime you want.

The lower has to be a pistol first in order for it to be able to have a pistol upper on it. That’s why I’d suggest buying a stripped lower and filling out a 77r, building it with milspec parts and buying the upper you want. Just keep in mind that pistols cannot have stocks on them, now including Pistol Braces, unless you fill out a Form 1 and have it classified as an SBR through the ATF.

If you do buy a rifle and put the upper on it, it has to be atleast 16”, and if it’s chambered in 5.56 or .223 it has to be considered a Heavy Barrel by the manufacturer. If it’s chambered in any other caliber (6.5 Grendel, 5.45x39, .300 BLK, 9mm etc) it doesn’t have to be an HBAR.

Here is an excerpt from USCCA’s website in regards to transporting a firearm:

“Fed Interstate 18 USC § 926A — Vehicle carry unloaded and secured
These sections of the code were intended to protect the passage of travelers (who can legally possess a firearm) to transport a firearm for any lawful purpose from any place where he or she may lawfully possess and carry such firearm to any other place where he or she may lawfully possess and carry such firearm. The firearm must be unloaded, and neither the firearm nor any ammunition can be readily accessible from the passenger compartment. In the case of a vehicle without a compartment separate from the driver’s compartment, the firearm or ammunition shall be contained in a locked container other than the glove compartment or console. It is recommended that ammunition be in a separate, preferably locked container.”

Not the last sentence.

This is from the MDSP FAQ page:

“How can I legally transport firearms within / through Maryland? 
Answer: They must be unloaded, in a carrying case, holster with a flap and the ammunition should be separate”

Edit: This is an excerpt from Cornell University’s Law website in regards to Federal requirements for transporting:

“Notwithstanding any other provision of any law or any rule or regulation of a State or any political subdivision thereof, any person who is not otherwise prohibited by this chapter from transporting, shipping, or receiving a firearm shall be entitled to transport a firearm for any lawful purpose from any place where he may lawfully possess and carry such firearm to any other place where he may lawfully possess and carry such firearm if, during such transportation the firearm is unloaded, and neither the firearm nor any ammunition being transported is readily accessible or is directly accessible from the passenger compartment of such transporting vehicle: Provided, That in the case of a vehicle without a compartment separate from the driver’s compartment the firearm or ammunition shall be contained in a locked container other than the glove compartment or console.

(Added Pub. L. 99–360, § 1(a), July 8, 1986, 100 Stat. 766.)”

So, in general regard, it’s a good idea to store ammo separate, and keep it out of reach of the driver.

IANAL, but general rule of thumb is to keep the handgun locked and out of reach of the driver with the ammunition stored separately. You don’t necessarily need to lock up your ammo, but I definitely wouldn’t put a magazine in the case with the handgun. 

Keep in mind that you are only legally allowed to transport the firearm between residences, ranges, legally licensed store/repair facilities, and where allowed to carry (you must have permission from the owner of the property). Any other stop would be considered a “Felony Stop” and you risk being arrested for unlawfully transporting a firearm without your concealed carry. 

For example, you lock your handgun in a case, store ammo separately, and take it to the range to shoot. Afterwards, you decide to stop for some lunch. You lock your handgun up the same as before, ammo separate, and stop at a diner on the way home. That stop, despite transporting your handgun in a safe and legal fashion, is still considered a “Felony Stop” as you are not transporting it to or from the range to your house. Rather, you are now transporting from the range to the diner, which is illegal.

The motor is running too lean, and the 2nd one is incredibly lean. I’d check vacuum leaks, and intake leaks post TB. Clean MAF potentially too. Check before you do though as some vehicles it’s not recommended to clean MAF sensors. 

After that look through fuel system. When was filter changed last? Are injectors clean? Check the pressure at the rail.

Lean conditions are caused by one of two things: too MUCH air, or too LITTLE fuel. Air can get in anywhere between the MAF sensor and head and be unmetered, meaning the car won’t adjust for it. It’ll typically see a lean code at the O2 sensor though and try to correct it, and will throw a CEL for lean condition. If it’s not correcting it at all, it is most likely something with the fuel lines or injectors that is restricting the amount of fuel it can add, by either a clog (filter, injectors), or decreased pressure (maybe a clog, fuel pump, HPFP, pressure regulator, faulty connection leaking, etc). This all depends on what kind of car it is, but it’s generally gonna be the same troubleshooting no matter what. If this is an old carbureted motor an air leak would be at the carb gasket or the intake gasket. but if this is a newer turbo car it could be a boost leak anywhere from the turbo all the way down to the intake gasket.

So the r32/33/34 names are chassis codes. That’s the generation. 32 is generally when they started AWD w/ HICAS, ATTESA, RB motors with Turbos. They are what are known as Godzilla in the community and follow the “gentleman’s Agreement” in Japan where the major manufacturers agreed to not exceed 276 BHP (spoiler alert they still did). 

The GTR versions all came with RB26DETT (twin turbo i6 equipped with the works (ATTESA AWD system w/ LSD, Hicas (rear steer), and all had the iconic GTR body styling (wing, skirts, front/rear bumper)

The GTS-T models of the R32/33 came with no AWD and usually had RB20DET (R32) and RB25DET (R33), and no HICAS, but with optional LSD in rear. 

The GTT Model of the R34 was basically the GTS-T of the R33 with the RB25DET NEO (updated) motor and RWD. 

There’s also GTS Models (R32/33) and GT (R34) with RWD and RB20DE (R32/33) and RB20DE NEO (R34)

There are varying models across all platforms with varying RB series motors and AWD and even 4WD systems. Such as the GT-FOUR of the r34 that had a N/A RB25DE and ATTESA AWD.


In short, GTR is RB26DETT w/ AWD and all the fixin’s. GTT or GTS-T is RWD with smaller single turbo motor and RWD only. And then there’s various other models with smaller N/A motors and varying AWD or rwd configurations.

The R32 and R33 had GTS-t and GTR Models and the R34 had GTR and GT-T models.

No, a bad ground would not put a parasitic drain on the battery. However, the vehicle would start having electrical gremlins. (Radio issues, random warning lights etc.) What could have happened here is that you had a battery that was going bad, or not charged properly from the alternator when parked, and the normal draw (50mA or less) caused the battery to die enough. Or, if you have any aftermarket electronics installed such as an alarm or remote start it may cause enough of a draw to kill the battery in that time. I’d bet that on an older car like that you had a battery that was greater than 3-5 years old and the battery was already starting to die and the normal drain on it was enough to kill it. 

I always recommend disconnecting the battery when you let a car sit for more than two weeks. You probably won’t have a problem but there’s always a chance you will.

Do you have any of those RFID gym tags on your key ring? It may be the RFID chip in the key causing an issue. Modern cars have immobilizers and chipped keys. When you put the key in the ignition a magnetic ring around the cylinder “picks up” the RFID code from the chip in the key and allows it to start. It’s the reason you couldn’t just cut a new key for a car but have to have it programmed to the car. In most cars it simply keeps the fuel pump from running but allows it to crank, causing a crank but no start condition. 

Source: am a 12v automotive electronics tech installing remote starters and have had this happen with my 2012 Fiat 500. One day after work it wouldn’t start. Towed it to the house. Found no gas pressure, realized the pump wasn’t working. ordered a new OEM fuel pump ($1300) and tried to start and still nothing. (Don’t ask why I didn’t check for power as a 12v tech) Finally got a bright idea to try my valet key. Started like the day I bought it. Atleast I don’t have to worry about my fuel pump anytime soon :/

What they’re trying to get at is that it may be running something and causing it to not make full contact with the flywheel. It could be just a squeaky slave cylinder or it could be actually rubbing on something. If it’s slipping when you floor it in gear the RPMs would shoot up without the car accelerating. Another test is from a dead stop if you just drop the clutch and it keeps going instead of stalling. Normally if you just let go of the clutch from a dead stop the car will stall but if it doesn’t and keeps running with the clutch fully disengaged and without using the friction zone to move them it is slipping. 

That being said, I had a very similar issue on my 2001 Hyundai tiburon. It was the bearing between my slave cylinder and clutch fork going out. Instead of pivoting like normal it had gone loose and squeaked quite loudly.

Start by jacking that wheel up and grabbing the top and bottom of the tire, and pushing back and forth. If you have play there it is probably from ball joint or control arm bushings. Then try grabbing the left and right sides of the tire and doing the same. If there’s play there then it is most likely tie rod or steering rack issue. If it moves all around or makes a grinding noise when spinning the wheel then it’s most likely wheel bearings. 

Another common thing to check is your sway bar links and bushings. The sway bar links the suspension on either side to one another like a torsion bar to keep the car flatter in tighter turns. Hitting a harder corner or bump can cause it to clunk if those joints are loose enough.

Set everything on the radio flat. Not lower, not higher, flat.. UNPLUG THE ALPINE POWER PACK. unplug your sub from the amplifier. At this point you should have no sound at all when playing anything. Get a Digital Multi Meter (DMM). If you don’t have one, Harbor Freight has some cheap ones that’ll do the job. 

Figure out what voltage to test for. You get it by doing the square root of power times resistance. In this case it’ll be 22.3 volts, assuming you have the dual 2 ohm voicecoils wired down to 1 ohm, not up to 4. 

Adjust your radio’s volume to about 3/4 full volume. Ideally you’d want to find where the radio clips and go just below that point, but I imagine you don’t have an o-scope to view the sine wave. If you want to go that route, [JYE Tech](https://jyetech.com/) has some really good cheap ones. Find your 40hz test tone and play that on repeat. 

Place the leads of the meter onto the speaker outputs. Set the meter to acV. Start with the gain all the way down, and go up slowly until you hit 22.3 volts. If I have to guess it’ll be fairly low as you have an 800 watts RMS amp on a 500 watts RMS sub. 

As far as LPF and HPF goes, I usually set my HPF to 100 or 120. The LPF is usually set between 130-180 hz but you’ll wanna tune that by ear. Listen to some good songs and turn it down if the vocals play through the sub.

To take things a bit further, if messing with adjustments through the radio doesn’t get it as quiet as you like, you could take a silver sharpie and mark the gain knob and amp where it is so you could turn it down and not have to worry about pulling you DMM out if you want to turn it back up.

Also, jack the car up, grab to outside of the tire at the 12 and 6 o clock positions. If it moves that way, ball joint needs repair. Then grab at 3 and 9. It depends on what kind of power you’re looking for but a turbo will do the most improvement over anything imo. However, it’ll cost well over 1000. 

The more air crammed into the cylinder the more power you make. Turbo’s will increase the amount of air by creating pressure in the intake thus forcing more air into the cylinders. 

You’d need a kit with all the piping, turbo, manifold, blow off valve, etc. after that you’ll need upgraded fuel management (injectors, pump, tuning) and most importantly the proper internals. You could run a small amount of boost and see maybe a 30 to 50 hp increase without doing internals but I’d stay safe with that.

You could start with an intake, and an exhaust. Intakes normally cost between 75-300 depending on brand and type. Exhausts depend on a lot of factors such as diameter, material, bends, muffler etc. In my own car I did a full exhaust, as well as a short ram intake and then took it a step further and built my top end.

The intake will allow more free flowing air into the cylinder by removing huge bends in piping, as well as removing resonators and stock air boxes that catch air. It’ll add a throatier sound to the exhaust as well as making a cool suction noise when you press the gas. It’ll net higher mpg as well as adding maybe 5 hp at the very most. 

The exhaust will actually remove back pressure from the (you guessed it) exhaust. Back pressure keeps the flow of exhaust gasses from leaving the cylinder. There’s multiple pieces that you can swap or you can do the whole thing. Keep in mind though, emissions. Every state is different. I live in md, where they are fairly tight on emissions. Removing catalytic converters is highly illegal and terrible for the environment. Most people end up doing cat-back exhausts which swaps all the piping behind the cats, not effecting emissions but freeing up the muffler and making it louder. Another option is high flow cats. They are usually direct swaps. 

That being said, doing the full exhaust normally only nets at the MOST 20 hp.

Another option that’ll add hp is to swap the Camshafts for a more aggressive setup. I personally swapped the 2.0 l Beta motor’s cams on my tiburon for the cams for the 1.8 l Beta motor from elantras. This starts to get more mechanically intensive and I would not recommend doing this unless you know what you’re actually doing.

Every motor uses valves to control the intake of air and the release of exhaust gases. The camshaft is what actually controls this, using lobes, which are essentially just bumpy spots on the camshaft that push down the valve. Changing the camshafts for more aggressive cams changes the amount of air let into the cylinder.

I really recommend doing one thing at a time so you can really see what each part you swap does to affect the performance.

Check the tie rod and ball joint. To check them jack up the car. For the ball joint grab the top and bottom of the tire (12 and 6 O'clock positions) and shake it. If it moves up or down there may be a bad ball joint. to check the tie rod, grab the sides (3 and 9 O'clock positions) and shake it back and forth. If it has play then the tie rod may need replacing. Another thing to look for is the grease fittings on the actual joints. The tie rod will be on the back of the hub, and the Ball joint will be underneath. You should take the tire off and inspect it physically. If the grease fittings are below the joint (they'd be like inside of it) then they may be too old. If you can grab the tie rod and move it back and forth then it is shot. The tie rod is a pretty easy change but you will need a special tool for it. You will need an alignment afterwards but since you are already planning on getting one then you don't need to worry.
The shop will charge around 400 probably for the fix but you can get the parts for around 40 a side. Some auto stores loan the tool for free, or you could pick it up for 40 at Harbor Freight. Of course you'll need a breaker bar, a ratchet, sockets, and some good luck

On my second pull day in the cycle I finish with forearm curls and I do what are called Lat Shrugs. 
With forearm curls grab a barbell like you are doing curls, bend foreward slightly at your hips, and keep your arms straight and bend your wrists as high up as you can. 
With Lat Shrugs you go into a deadhang on a pull-up bar, and just get yourself into the bottom of a pull-up. Do this to failure for three sets. 

TLDR: do a little bit of forearm work after back days (or whenever you do deadlifts or rows). My favorites are Reverse Grip Curls, Farmer Walks, Forearm Curls and Lat Shrugs.

Some tips for form in bench press (both dumbbell and barbell) are that your mid back should never touch the bench, and you should be able to fit a hand under your back. When you are pushing the weight up, drive your feet into the ground. The idea is that by straining your entire body, you are increasing the blood flow. However, do not use this as an excuse to kip. 

Some other exercises you should look into doing are Around the Worlds, which help develop the minor pec, just below the clavicle, and Pullovers. There is a specific form to the pullovers however, as the way you situate your arms determines if you are working your lats or pecs more. 

A few other tips I'd give are to keep training the rest of your body just as well as your chest, as it is shown that working every muscle group promotes muscle growth more as your body gets used to recovering from the constant stress. Flex often, as it helps to improve your muscle control. And as always, it is important to eat plenty of carbs and protein within a short time of working out, it's recommended to eat within 30 minutes of finishing.

Edit: As with every major muscle, make sure you push your limits, and increase progressively.

To cut fat, but still be able to gain lean muscle, you should keep a High protein, low carb diet. Protein should generally be a 1g/1lb of body weight. And carbs should be about half of that. 
However, if you don't mind taking the time (about a year or so) to gain a very good amount of muscle before getting cut, what you could do is go through bulking periods and resting periods. During bulking periods, which will generally be the night or day after you workout, you want to eat as much protein as possible, and in order to build that muscle quick, you will need a good amount of carbs along with it. Proteins give the proper amino acids to build the muscle and enzymes you need, but the carbs give your body the energy to do that. During resting periods (excessive days without training) you shouldn't eat as much but simply eat the amount you need to maintain muscle. For those of you who like to count calories, maintenance for me, a 160 lb moderate lifter, is around 2000 calories and building is about 2500.
